$comment: The projects the harness deploys, and what each one is here to prove.
Every repo is a FORK we own, whose default branch `bench` is frozen at the sha
below. That is not belt-and-braces: lib/deploy-pipeline.ts clones with
`git clone --depth 1 <url>` and no ref, so it always takes the default branch's
HEAD. Against an upstream repo the corpus would silently change the first time
anybody merged anything, and every number taken before that would become
uncomparable with every number after — without a single line of this file
changing. Freezing the branch is what makes the sha mean something.
`expect.outcome` is deliberately "unknown" for most of them. Nobody has run
these through the platform yet, and writing down a guess would turn the first
batch from a measurement into a self-graded exam. The first batch ESTABLISHES
the baseline; `bench/calibrate.ts` writes what actually happened back into this
file, a human looks at it, and only then does a later batch get to call a

projects.why: Next.js output:'export' that fails on next/image. The one case already known end to end: the static lane needs out/index.html, and a repair agent that removes output:'export' can never pass. Lane-awareness regressions show up here first.
A large real Vite SPA. Exercises the static lane's SPA fallback in verify-app.ts and a build heavy enough that build-cache behaviour is visible.
Server-rendered Next.js as people actually write it. The most common shape the product sees.
Remix with Prisma and a migration step — a real app whose build is not the whole story, because something has to run before traffic.
The heavy end of the same shape: Postgres, migrations, a release command. This is where release-job.ts and pg-role.ts are actually exercised.

Python, and a repo with a backend and a frontend side by side. Two questions at once: can we run uvicorn at all, and does a two-app repo get planned or refused. Python is also the language whose run command cannot be guessed.
A Go HTTP service with no Dockerfile at the repo root — so this measures the Go detector and the buildpack path, not our ability to run someone else's Dockerfile.

The only project here with a real Procfile: `web:` and `worker:`. It is the one case that reaches the worker-pool half of lib/processes.ts and awaitRunning() rather than fleetProbe() — a branch of the code no other project in this corpus touches. It also wants Redis, so it doubles as the dependency-refusal case.

Dozens of independent implementations in one tree. It is in the corpus BECAUSE it should be refused: repo-facts.ts/refusalReason exists for exactly this, and a benchmark where everything passes cannot notice the day the refusal path breaks and starts deploying something arbitrary instead.
projects.$budgetNote: 600, not the 120 this was written with (see $budgets). 120 encoded the assumption that a refusal is instant — no clone, no build, just repo-facts.ts saying no. On 10 Aug the harness gave up here at 120s and the server said `building`: the refusal had not happened, and a budget below the ~231s a real deploy takes cannot tell `never` from `not yet`. That made it a measurement of our own patience. The EXPECTATION is deliberately untouched — this repo should still be refused, and that it was not is the finding, not the budget.

projects.why: Ours, and deliberately broken. The repair agent's own case: does it fix it, in how many redeploys, for how many tokens. Deployed from a folder rather than a URL, which is also the only project here that exercises the upload door.

$budgets: Raised on 10 Aug from guesses to measurements. Every original number was
written before a single deploy had been timed, and five of the ten were below
the deploy they were timing: excalidraw, outline, next-enterprise and
indie-stack were all still building when the harness gave up, and
next-enterprise had already built its image and was deploying it.
The floor is now 600s because a cold deploy of a real application on this
platform costs 4-10 minutes — broken went live in 239s, and it is one of the
smallest things here. The ceiling is 1200s to match BUILD_TIMEOUT: past that
the server has given up too, so waiting longer measures nothing.
